analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 15% minimum tax on large corporations' financial statement income.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on May 11, 2023 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the corporate alternative minimum tax, which requires companies that report more than $1 billion in profits to their shareholders to pay at least 15% of those book profits in taxes, even if deductions and credits reduce their taxable income to less. Repealing it would mean those large corporations pay less federal tax. The bill was introduced by Senator Barrasso with ten Republican cosponsors and was sent to the Finance Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Very large corporations — those reporting over $1 billion in profits to shareholders — would pay less in federal taxes, since the 15% minimum on their financial-statement income would no longer apply, retroactive to tax years beginning after December 31, 2022 [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporations with over $1B in reported profits

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 15% alternative minimum tax applied to the financial statement (book) income of corporations that report over $1 billion in profits to their shareholders [S2][S3].
Applies the repeal to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022, so corporations would get the benefit retroactively for the 2023 tax year onward [S3].

Also removes the corporate minimum tax from related rules, such as the limitation on the general business credit and estimated tax calculations, eliminating the compliance and payment obligations tied to it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through reduced government revenue: the tax being repealed is one of the few that ensures the largest, most profitable corporations pay at least 15% on reported profits, and repealing it removes that revenue from the Treasury. Companies with large tax credits that had begun paying the minimum would see the biggest savings.

drawbacks.text: The tax being repealed is aimed at corporations that report over $1 billion in profits to shareholders; repealing it lets those companies keep income they would otherwise owe tax on, reducing federal revenue that funds services ordinary people rely on [S2][S3].

Supporters' strongest objection: the tax is levied on financial statement income rather than taxable income, so a company can owe it even in a year when tax credits or deductions push its taxable income near zero — critics say that amounts to taxing profits that don't exist on a tax-return basis (general policy knowledge; the bill text confirms the tax is based on financial statement income [S3]).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely to a small set of very large corporations, while the cost — lost federal revenue — is spread across everyone who depends on or pays for government. Whatever the design criticisms of taxing book income, this bill removes the floor ensuring billion-dollar-profit companies pay at least 15% on reported profits, with no replacement revenue in the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it simply expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Barrasso introduced the bill on May 11, 2023 with ten Republican cosponsors [S1][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which was its only committee referral [S1][S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history — no hearing, no markup, no vote — through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large corporations subject to the 15% minimum tax are better off, since they continue to owe it; the Treasury keeps the revenue it would have lost if the repeal had passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations keep paying; revenue preserved

sides.party_line_note: All eleven sponsors were Republicans; the Democratic majority that controlled the Senate Finance Committee never scheduled any action on the bill, and no vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Corporations with over $1 billion in financial statement income
industries.note: The bill would exempt them from the 15% minimum tax on reported profits, letting deductions and credits reduce their effective rate on large profits. The cost is spread to the Treasury and taxpayers at large, while the benefit is concentrated among the biggest corporations.
